lectures.title: The Supreme Court: establishment, Chief Justice and judges

items: **Constitutional framework:** The Supreme Court and its Judges are governed under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147).
**Federal Court:** established under the Government of India Act, 1935 (1 Oct 1937); first CJ: **Sir Maurice Gwyer**.

**Inauguration & predecessor:** the Supreme Court was inaugurated on **28 January 1950**; it succeeded both the Federal Court of India (established under the Government of India Act, 1935) and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
**Strength & Parliament's power:** the power to increase the number of Supreme Court judges is vested exclusively in Parliament by law (Art. 124(1)).
**Seat of the Supreme Court (Art. 130):** Delhi (or other places decided by the CJI with the President's approval).
**Constitutional status:** Head of the Union Judiciary and the Supreme Court of India under Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147).
**Appointment:** appointed by the President of India under Article 124(2); by convention, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is appointed as Chief Justice of India (CJI).
**Tenure & retirement:** holds office until attaining the age of 65 years (no fixed term in years).
**Oath:** administered by the President (or a person appointed by the President) under the Third Schedule.
**Resignation:** addressed in writing to the President of India.
**Longest-serving CJI:** Justice **Y.V. Chandrachud** (16th CJI; served 22 Feb 1978 – 11 July 1985; over 7 years).
**Shortest-serving CJI:** Justice **Kamal Narain Singh** (served 25 Nov 1991 – 12 Dec 1991; 18 days).
**Appointing authority:** Supreme Court Judges are appointed exclusively by the President of India by warrant under hand and seal (Art. 124).
**Art. 124(2):** Judges are formally appointed by the President of India based on the binding recommendations of the Collegium.
**Distinguished jurist rule:** a distinguished jurist is eligible to be appointed a Supreme Court Judge (Art. 124(3)(c)).
**Oath of a Supreme Court Judge:** governed by Article 124(6); administered by the President of India (or a person appointed by him).
**First woman Judge of the Supreme Court:** Justice **M. Fathima Beevi** (1989); also the first Muslim woman in the higher judiciary.

parts.t: Acting Chief Justice, ad hoc judges and retired judges
items: **Acting CJI (Art. 126):** appointed by the President when the office of CJI is vacant, the CJI is absent or is unable to perform duties.
**Ad hoc Judge (Art. 127):** appointed by the CJI (with the previous consent of the President and consultation with the concerned HC Chief Justice) to meet a lack of quorum.
**Retired Judges at SC sittings (Art. 128):** attendance of retired Judges; the CJI requests with the prior consent of the President.

parts.t: Retirement, resignation and life after retirement
items: **Retirement age:** Supreme Court Judges retire at **65 years** of age (Art. 124(2)); no fixed tenure in years, a Judge retires strictly upon turning 65.
**Resignation:** a Supreme Court Judge addresses a written resignation directly to the President of India (Art. 124(2)(a)).
**Post-retirement pleading:** complete bar (Art. 124(7)); a Supreme Court Judge cannot practice in ANY court / authority in India.
**Transfer provision:** not applicable to a Supreme Court Judge.

**Salaries (Art. 125):** salaries, allowances and rights of Supreme Court Judges (incl. CJI); determined by Parliament by law; salary, allowances and pension are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable).

parts.t: Removal of a Supreme Court judge
items: **Removal procedure (Art. 124(4)):** removed by an order of the President after an address by Parliament.
**Majority required:** Special Majority in each House (majority of total membership, i.e. ≥ 50% of total strength, + ≥ 2/3 of members present and voting) in the same session.
**Procedure:** governed procedurally by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.

**Removal vs appointment:** the President appoints SC judges in consultation / collegium concurrence, but removal requires a statutory inquiry + parliamentary special majority address under Art. 124(4).

lectures.title: The Supreme Court: jurisdiction and special powers

items: **Original & exclusive jurisdiction (Art. 131):** exclusive jurisdiction over direct federal disputes involving a legal right.
Centre ↔ one or more States (≥ 1 State)
**Not covered:** political questions without legal rights; pre-Constitution treaties / agreements (Art. 131 proviso); inter-State water disputes (Art. 262).
**Also not covered under Article 131:** Finance Commission matters (Art. 280) and recovery of damages by a private party against the Union.
**Writ jurisdiction (Art. 32):** Fundamental Right to approach the SC directly for enforcement of Part III rights (Fundamental Rights).
**Writs issued:** Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
**Scope:** SC writ scope is narrower than that of the High Courts (Art. 226 covers FRs + legal rights); Article 32 covers Fundamental Rights ONLY.
The SC cannot refuse an Art. 32 petition (it is itself a Fundamental Right).
**First PIL considered:** Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).
Appeals from High Court judgments involving a substantial question of law as to interpretation of the Constitution
Requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A
Appeals in civil proceedings involving a substantial question of law of general importance
High Court must certify under Art. 134A that the question needs SC determination
Appeals in criminal proceedings where HC reversed acquittal to death sentence or withdrew trial to itself
Available as of right in capital punishment reversals without HC certificate
**SLP (Art. 136):** discretionary appellate power to grant leave to appeal from any judgment / order of any court / tribunal.
**Armed Forces exception (Art. 136(2)):** SLPs do NOT lie against judgments / sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals (Military Tribunals / Armed Forces Courts).
**Advisory jurisdiction (Art. 143):** the President refers questions of law / fact of public importance for the Court's opinion (Presidential reference).
**Art. 143(1):** on a question of law / public importance, the SC may tender or refuse advice (may tender opinion).
**Art. 143(2):** on pre-Constitution disputes (pre-constitutional matters), the SC is bound to give advice (must tender opinion).
In all cases the advice tendered is strictly advisory and NOT binding on the President.

parts.t: Review, binding precedent and complete justice
items: **Review jurisdiction (Art. 137):** power of the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders; distinct from Judicial Review of statutes; subject to Parliamentary law and Court rules.
**Article 141 (Binding Precedent):** the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India.

**Article 142 (Complete Justice):** empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing "Complete Justice" in any cause or matter pending before it; operates unhindered by ordinary statutory limitations.
**Article 142, nature:** inherent equitable jurisdiction (distinct from Judicial Review).
**Curative Petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra, 2002):** evolved by the Supreme Court under its inherent powers anchored in Article 142.
**Purpose of the Curative Petition:** to prevent abuse of process and cure gross miscarriages of justice after a review petition under Article 137 has been dismissed.

parts.t: Constitution Bench and Court of Record
items: **Constitution Bench (Article 145(3)):** minimum **5 Judges** required to hear any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution or for references under Article 143.
**Court of Record (Art. 129):** judgments / decisions have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any subordinate court.
**Contempt:** as a Court of Record the Supreme Court has inherent power to punish for contempt of itself.
**High Court (Art. 215):** parallel Court of Record status at the State level.

lectures.title: The Collegium system and the NJAC

items: **Core mandate:** the institutional system governing the appointment and transfer of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.

**Origin & status:** it is NOT a constitutional body (not expressly mentioned in the Constitution) and was NOT created by an Act of Parliament; it is a judicially evolved system developed through Supreme Court rulings.
**Appointing authority (Art. 124(2) & 217(1)):** Judges are formally appointed by the President of India based on the binding recommendations of the Collegium.
**Functional scope:** covers both Appointments (Supreme Court & High Courts) and Transfers (High Court Judges).
**First Judges Case** (S.P. Gupta v. Union of India)
"Consultation" does NOT mean "concurrence"; established Executive primacy (executive supremacy) in judicial appointments
**Second Judges Case** (SCAORA v. Union of India)
Reversed the 1981 ruling; "consultation" means concurrence; established Judicial primacy
Clarified procedural working; CJI's opinion must reflect a plural consultation with senior colleagues
**Second Judges Case (1993):** formally birthed (introduced) the Collegium system: CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges.
**Third Judges Case (1998):** expanded the SC Collegium to CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges for SC appointments.
**99th Amendment & NJAC (2014–15):** the National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down as unconstitutional to preserve the Independence of the Judiciary (Basic Structure).
**Supreme Court appointments & elevations:** CJI + 4 senior-most SC Judges (Total = 5 members).
**High Court appointments:** recommendation initiated by the Chief Justice of the HC + 2 senior-most HC judges; forwarded to the Supreme Court Collegium (CJI + 2 senior-most SC Judges).
**High Court transfers:** requisite consultation involves CJI + 4 senior-most SC Judges + Chief Justices of both High Courts (transferring and receiving).

parts.t: Collegium system compared with the NJAC
items: Judicially evolved through Supreme Court case law
CJI (Chairperson); 2 Senior SC Judges; Union Law Minister; 2 Eminent Persons (nominated by PM + CJI + LoP)
Law Minister was a permanent member
Struck down as unconstitutional in 2015 (4th Judges Case) for violating Independence of the Judiciary
**"Parliament created the Collegium by law":** FALSE (judicially created).
**"Collegium is expressly mentioned in Article 124":** FALSE; it is not explicitly written in the Constitution.
**Functional scope:** the Collegium deals with Appointments AND Transfers (NOT appointments alone).
**Genesis:** judicially evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1st Case: 1981, 2nd Case: 1993, 3rd Case: 1998).

**Definition:** the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary (constitutional courts) to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders / actions, declaring them void if they contravene constitutional provisions.
**Exercising authority:** vested jointly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) (NOT the Supreme Court alone).
**Borrowed source:** adopted from the USA; the doctrine was first propounded in **Marbury v. Madison, 1803** by Chief Justice John Marshall.

**Constitutional Supremacy vs Parliamentary Sovereignty:** India has Constitutional Supremacy with Judicial Review; the UK has Parliamentary Sovereignty (no traditional judicial review of primary parliamentary legislation).
Marbury v. Madison (1803) (Chief Justice John Marshall, USA)
Power of the higher judiciary (SC + HCs) to adjudicate on the constitutional validity of legislative acts and executive actions
Primary textual foundation; laws abridging Fundamental Rights are void pro tanto
Express constitutional basis for striking down ultra vires laws
Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights enforcement
Constitutional remedy & part of the Basic Structure
High Court writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights + any other legal right
Supreme Court's power to review its own judgments or orders
Art. 137 Review (review of own judgment) is distinct from Judicial Review
Power of Supreme Court to pass decrees / orders for "Complete Justice"
Inherent equitable jurisdiction (distinct from Judicial Review)
**Not a policy review:** it is NOT the court questioning the political wisdom, policy merits, or advisability of legislation.
**Not pre-assent scrutiny:** it is NOT automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills.
**Not an appeal:** it is NOT an ordinary appellate proceeding.

**Federal, not unitary:** Judicial Review reinforces the Federal principle (preserves constitutional distribution of powers and enforces constitutional limits); it is NOT a Unitary element (unlike All India Services, Governor's appointment, or emergency provisions).

lectures.title: High Courts: structure, judges and jurisdiction

items: **Constitutional framework:** governed under Part VI, Chapter V (Articles 214–231); Article 214 mandates a High Court for each State.
**Indian High Courts Act, 1861:** in **1862** the first three High Courts were established at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
**1866:** High Court for North-Western Provinces established at Agra (shifted to Allahabad in 1869).
**Strength (Art. 216):** the strength / number of judges for each High Court is decided and fixed by the President of India (NOT Parliament, NOT the Governor / Chief Minister).
High Courts to be Courts of Record (evidentiary value + power to punish for contempt)
Constitution / composition of High Courts (Chief Justice + judges appointed by President)
Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court
Application of certain provisions relating to Supreme Court (Removal) to High Courts
Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge
Salaries, allowances, and pensions of Judges
Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another by the President
Appointment of Additional / Acting Judges & attendance of retired Judges
Power of High Courts to issue certain Writs
Power of Superintendence over all courts and tribunals by the High Court
Extension of jurisdiction of High Courts to Union Territories
Establishment of a Common High Court for two or more States / UTs

**Appointing authority:** High Court Judges are appointed by the President of India by warrant under hand and seal (Art. 217), NOT the Governor; the Governor has NO power to appoint High Court Judges.
**Chief Justice of HC (Art. 217):** appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI + Governor of the State.
**Other HC Judges (Art. 217):** appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI + Governor + Chief Justice of that High Court.
**Qualifications (Art. 217(2)):** citizen of India AND held a judicial office in India for ≥ 10 years OR practiced as an advocate of a High Court for ≥ 10 years.
Unlike the Supreme Court (Art. 124(3)(c)), there is NO provision for appointing a "distinguished jurist" as a High Court judge.
**Oath:** governed by Article 217(1) / 219; administered by the Governor of the State (Art. 219).
**Resignation:** submitted (addressed) to the President of India (Art. 217(1)(a)).
**Retirement age:** **62 years** (Article 217(1)); raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th CAA, 1963; applies to Additional / Acting Judges under Art. 224(3).
**Transfer (Article 222):** transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another by the President, on CJI-led Collegium advice.

**Removal (Art. 217(1)(b) r/w Art. 124(4); Art. 218):** removed ONLY by an order of the President following an Address passed by each House of Parliament by a Special Majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

**Post-retirement practice (Art. 220):** a retired permanent HC Judge CANNOT plead / act before any court or authority in India, EXCEPT the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they did not serve as a permanent judge).
**Determining authority:** salaries and allowances of High Court Judges (incl. CJ) are determined by Parliament by law (Art. 221).
**Salary & allowances:** charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202(3)(d)).
**Pension:** charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)); NOT the State Fund.
**Acting Chief Justice (Art. 223):** appointed by the President from among HC Judges when the office of Chief Justice is vacant, temporarily absent, or unable to perform duties.

**Additional Judges (Art. 224(1)):** appointed by the President due to temporary increase in court business or arrears of work for a period not exceeding 2 years (cannot serve beyond 62 years of age).
**Acting Judges (Art. 224(2)):** appointed by the President when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent or acting as Chief Justice (ceases at 62 years).

**Retired Judges at High Court sittings (Art. 224A):** the Chief Justice of a High Court (with the President's prior consent) may request a retired Judge of that High Court or of any other High Court to sit and act as a High Court Judge.

**Writ scope (Art. 226 > Art. 32):** High Court writ jurisdiction is broader in scope than the Supreme Court because it extends to Fundamental Rights + any other legal purpose / right (ordinary legal rights).
**Discretion:** High Court writ power is discretionary; Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
**Supervisory jurisdiction (Art. 227):** the High Court exercises administrative and judicial superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction.
**Armed Forces exception (Art. 227(4)):** superintendence does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
**Advisory jurisdiction:** NO; High Courts have no general advisory powers.

parts.t: Chief Justice of a High Court: judicial and administrative capacity
items: **Administrative capacity:** when acting in an administrative capacity (e.g., staff appointments, disciplinary actions), the Chief Justice of a High Court is subject to the writ jurisdiction (Art. 226) of another Judge of that same High Court.
**No absolute immunity:** the Chief Justice enjoys no absolute immunity from judicial review regarding administrative decisions.

parts.t: Common High Courts and territorial jurisdiction (Articles 230 & 231)
items: **Article 231:** Parliament has the power to establish a Common High Court for two or more States and UTs.
Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu
Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh

lectures.title: Supreme Court and High Court compared

items: Salary: State Fund; Pension: Union CFI

parts.t: The judges compared: appointment, oath, resignation
items: President of India by warrant (Art. 217); NOT Governor
NOT eligible (no provision for distinguished jurist)
Article 222 (by President on CJI-led Collegium advice)
**High Court Judge:** oath administered by the Governor; resignation addressed to the President.

parts.t: The judges compared: retirement, removal and after
items: 62 Years (Article 217(1)); raised from 60 to 62 by 15th CAA, 1963
Order of President following an Address by Parliament (Art. 124(4))
Order of President following an Address by Parliament (Art. 217(1))
Permitted ONLY in SC and other High Courts (Art. 220)

**Removal (common rule):** both SC and HC Judges are removed only by an order of the President following an Address by each House of Parliament supported by a Special Majority (≥ 50% total strength + ≥ 2/3rd present and voting) on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Arts. 124(4) & 218).

**Post-retirement practice:** a Supreme Court Judge cannot practice in ANY court / authority in India; a High Court Judge can practice in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (where they were not a permanent judge).
High Court Judges (Art. 217) + State PSC Members (Art. 316(2))
Supreme Court Judges (Art. 124) + UPSC Members (Art. 316(2)) + CAG + CEC / ECs
**Charged status (Art. 112 / 202):** Supreme Court Judges: charged on CFI (non-votable); High Court Judges: salary charged on State CF, pension charged on Union CFI.

**Dual-fund rule for High Court Judges:** salary & allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 202(3)(d)); pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3)(d)(iii)).
**Articles:** Article 125: salaries, allowances, and rights of Supreme Court Judges; Article 221: salaries and allowances of High Court Judges.
